title: Precision Measurement of Radioactivity in Gamma-Rays Spectrometry Using HPGe Detectors
author: Joel, Penabei, et al.

steps.title: Collect composite soil samples
steps.instruction: Randomly select 18 composite soil samples from the two University of Douala campuses (7 from Campus 1 ESSEC, 11 from Campus 2 Ndong‑Bong). At each sampling point clear the near‑vertical surface, record GPS coordinates, collect four subsamples at the edges and one at the centre within a 5 m² area, each at approximately 20 cm depth, and space each composite location about 300 m from the others. Mix the five subsamples thoroughly to form one composite and place it in a polyethylene bag.

steps.title: Dry and homogenize samples
steps.instruction: Air‑dry the bagged composites for one week, then oven‑dry at 105 °C for 24 h. Grind the dried material to a fine powder and sieve through a 2 mm wire mesh to obtain uniform particle size.

steps.title: Seal samples for secular equilibrium
steps.instruction: Pack the powdered sample into a 120 mL airtight polyethylene cylindrical container, record the dry weight, and store the sealed container for 32 days to allow secular equilibrium between ²²⁶Ra and its daughter nuclides.

steps.title: Set up and calibrate Douala detector
steps.instruction: Place the BEGe‑6530 broad‑energy germanium detector in a 10 cm thick Canberra Model 747 lead shield. Perform energy and efficiency calibration using the built‑in Multiport II multichannel analyzer. Record detector resolution values (≈0.5 keV at 5.9 keV, 0.75 keV at 122 keV, 2.2 keV at 1332 keV) and note peak‑to‑Compton ratios of 25–40.

steps.title: Count samples with Douala detector
steps.instruction: Insert each sealed sample into the BEGe‑6530 spectrometer and count for 86 400 s (24 h) to obtain peak‑area statistics >0.1 %. Process the spectra with Genie‑2000 software version 3.2 applying the cascade‑summing correction coefficient.

steps.title: Set up and calibrate Liege detector
steps.instruction: Configure the HPGe GC0818‑7600SL detector (active diameter 43 mm, 30 % relative efficiency at 1.33 MeV, resolution 1.88 keV at 1.33 MeV) inside its shielding. Carry out absolute photo‑peak efficiency calibration using a standard multi‑gamma 152Eu source placed in planar beakers of the same geometry as the samples, with the radionuclides dispersed in gel matrices surrounding the detector. Acquire the calibration spectra for 7 200 s (2 h).

steps.title: Count samples with Liege detector
steps.instruction: Measure each sealed sample with the HPGe system for 86 400 s (24 h).

steps.title: Measure background with empty container
steps.instruction: Count an empty polystyrene container under the same geometry and counting time as the samples. Use this spectrum to subtract background from the sample spectra.

steps.title: Calculate activity concentrations
steps.instruction: From the background‑subtracted spectra extract full‑energy peak areas for the following gamma lines: (a) ²²⁶Ra – weighted mean of 214Pb (295.1 keV, 351.9 keV), 214Bi (609.3 keV, 1120.29 keV) and 186.2 keV (corrected for 185.7 keV ²³⁵U interference); (b) ²³²Th – 228Ac (338.4 keV, 911.2 keV, 969.11 keV) and 212Pb (238.6 keV); (c) ⁴⁰K – 1460.8 keV (10.7 % intensity). Convert net counts to activity (Bq kg⁻¹) using the calibrated efficiencies and the recorded dry mass of each sample.

description: Gamma-ray spectrometry is a non-destructive technics used to gauge electromagnetic radiation in the gamma-ray spectrum of radioactive sources. This is performed through the procedure of the counting and measuring the energy of individual photon emitted from different elements present in soil. The use of germanium detectors in high-resolution gamma-ray spectrometry is a standout amongst the most generally utilized strategies for the identification and quantification of unknown gamma-ray emitting radionuclides in sample [1], [2]. The estimation of gamma rays is valuable for the determination of the elemental sample composition of a wide assortment of sources. The measured energy of a gamma-ray corresponds to the type of element and its isotope, while the number of counts corresponds to the abundance of the radioactive source present in the measured sample with some little considerations. The process of measuring a gamma ray begins at the radioactive source, which emits high energy photons during its unstable radioactive decay [3]. This spectrometry technique requires earlier learning of the photo-peak efficiency of the detector in the counting geometry for each photon energy. In any case, measures crevices with various equipment in gamma spectrometry are nowadays a real challenge for scientists: to locate the most efficiency and enhance the measurement time in the lab and the statistic is not always obvious device [4]. That is the framework in which this study is part which consists of a double measure of natural radioactivity present in soil from two campuses of the University of Douala. A first step of this study was made in Cameroon with a Broad Energy Germanium detector (BEGE-6530 model) and a second with an HPGe (GC0818-7600SL model) detector took place at the Laboratory of Nuclear Physics of the University of Liege in Belgium.
